Evelyn N

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: There is nothing to win: move the corners of a polygon and watch a chain of circles, each touching the last one and two sides of the shape.
How to play: Drag a corner or the yellow point, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Use the side buttons to change the shape and the pair buttons to colour two circles.
Sides: 3
Look for the math

Evelyn's original page is about a triangle and six circles. This applet extends the same chain to a polygon with 3 to 21 sides. The page makes several claims about how long the chain can be; the logic test checked them over every offered size and many starting positions, and two of them do not hold for what the applet actually draws.

Building the next circle

At corner A, the dashed line is the angle bisector; it meets the diagonal between A's neighbours at L. Put the centre of a circle at A + t(L − A). Its distance to the next side is t × d, where d is the distance from L to that side, so that circle is tangent to both sides through A. Tangency to the previous circle gives u t² + 2v t + w = 0. The applet's Solve2 returns (−v ± √(v² − uw)) / u and prefers the root between 0 and 1, which is what this port computes. The test checked that each drawn circle really touches the one before it.

How long is the chain?

The page says that for odd n the chain has at most 2n circles. The applet's loop stops after 2n by construction, so it never displays more, but continuing its own formula can produce another circle: the bound is the program's cap here, not something the test can prove from the drawing. For a regular polygon, the chain returns to its first circle after n circles when n is even and after 2n when n is odd. The page also allows a length of n + 1; that never appeared in the full sweep of starting positions.

Where the page and the applet part company

The page says that for even n the distance between the 1st and the 2n-th circle does not depend on the first radius. In the applet it plainly does: for a square, moving P changes that distance from about 99 to 145 board units. The page also says an inscriptible quadrilateral closes after n circles; the regular square does, but the sampled irregular cyclic quadrilaterals stay open. The logic test asserts what the code does rather than repeating those sentences.

Back to Evelyn's triangle

Set the sides to 3 and the chain has six circles; the sixth touches the first. That is the six circles theorem on Evelyn's page. Changing the number of sides changes the period from six to the polygon's own count, and the colour picker marks the pair of neighbours the applet is emphasizing.

Set the sides to 4 and watch the fifth circle land on the first; then set the sides to 5 and see why it takes ten.
